slides.0.title: Cost structure and pricing
slides.0.subtitle: Only part of the shelf price is the wine itself
slides.1.title: The cost of a bottle
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Vineyard costs
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Capital for land and planting, labour, sprays and equipment; steep, hand-worked slopes (Mosel, Douro, Wachau) cost far more per hectare than flat, mechanised land, and low yields spread that over fewer bottles
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Winery and maturation costs
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Equipment, energy, barrels (new oak is expensive), and the capital and storage tied up during ageing; the longer the ageing, the longer money is locked up, one reason Vintage Port, Barolo and prestige Champagne cost more
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Packaging, transport and tax
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Glass, closure, label, carton and freight are the biggest share in cheap wine; in many markets (such as the UK) duty is a fixed amount per bottle or per unit of alcohol, so the value of the wine itself in a cheap bottle is very small
slides.1.content: Fixed costs (duty, packaging) make cheap wine poor value and mean premium bottles contain a higher share of wine value.
slides.2.title: Mark-ups along the price chain
slides.2.highlights.0.title: From winery to consumer
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Cellar-door price → importer or wholesaler mark-up → retailer or restaurant mark-up → taxes; every tier needs a margin, so shelf prices are often several times the ex-cellar price
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Mark-ups in the on-trade
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Restaurants carry service, glassware, stock and premises costs, so mark-ups are usually higher than retail; expensive wines often get a lower multiple so prices do not scare guests away
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Bulk and bottled
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Bulk wine is priced by the litre on thin margins, and bottling in the destination market saves freight and glass weight; bottled wine can build brands and premiums. South African and Chilean exports, where volume is bulk and value is bottled, follow this logic
slides.2.content: When discussing price, first ask which tier of the chain takes the money.
slides.3.title: Pricing strategies
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Cost-plus pricing
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Cost plus a fixed margin: simple, but it ignores what the market will pay; common in bulk and private-label wine
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Value and prestige pricing
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Pricing on perceived value: scores, scarcity, brand heritage and classification (Bordeaux classed growths, Grand Cru) push prices far above cost; pricing too low can actually damage the image
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Price points and positioning
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Retail is tiered by psychological price points (e.g. £5, £10, £20 in the UK); brands must choose a price tier and hold it, because constant promotions teach consumers to buy only on deal
slides.3.content: The heart of Diploma business questions: price is a compromise between cost, competition and perceived value.
slides.4.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge check
In markets with per-bottle duty, why is the wine’s own value so small in a cheap bottle?
A. Grapes for cheap wine cost more
B. Duty and packaging are fixed costs and take a big share
C. Cheap wine has more alcohol
D. Cheap wine has no freight cost
Fixed costs weigh heaviest on cheap wine.
Why does long ageing push prices up?
A. Ageing increases volume
B. Aged wine needs no packaging
C. Capital and storage are tied up longer
D. Aged wine is tax-free
Capital and storage costs must be reflected in the price.
What is the main advantage of bulk wine bottled in the destination market?
A. Commands the highest premium
B. Escapes all taxes
C. Must be single-vineyard
D. Saves freight and glass weight
Bulk margins are thin; it wins on logistics efficiency.
Which strategy mainly drives the prices of top classed growths?
A. Value and prestige pricing
B. Cost-plus pricing
C. Bulk quotation
D. Permanent promotional pricing
Scarcity, scores and history push prices far above cost.
